chapter.title: The present tense of regular -er verbs

sections.title: -er verbs with spelling and stem changes
When is the present tense used in French?

grammar_rules.title: Formation of regular -er verbs in the present tense
grammar_rules.summary: Drop -er from the infinitive and add endings: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
grammar_rules.explanation: To conjugate a regular -er verb in the present tense, remove the infinitive ending -er to find the stem, then add the endings corresponding to the subject pronoun.
exceptions: spelling/stem changing -er verbs have minor adjustments
notes: The endings -e, -es, and -ent are all silent in spoken French.

common_mistakes.explanation: The 3rd person plural ending -ent is completely silent.

grammar_rules.title: Spelling change in verbs ending in -ger
grammar_rules.summary: Keep the 'e' before -ons in the 'nous' form to preserve the soft 'g' sound (mangeons).
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs ending in -ger (like manger, voyager, nager, partager), add an 'e' before the -ons ending of nous (nous mangeons, nous voyageons) to keep the soft 'g' sound.

steps: In the nous form, retain 'e' after 'g' before 'ons'

notes: Only the nous form is affected in the present tense.

common_mistakes.explanation: Without 'e', 'g' would sound hard as in 'gant'.

grammar_rules.title: Spelling change in verbs ending in -cer
grammar_rules.summary: Change 'c' to 'ç' before -ons in the 'nous' form to preserve the soft 's' sound (commençons).
grammar_rules.explanation: For verbs ending in -cer (like commencer, avancer, lancer, remplacer), change 'c' to 'ç' before the 'o' in nous (nous commençons) to keep the soft 's' sound.

steps: In the nous form, change 'c' to 'ç' before 'ons'

notes: Only the nous form is affected in the present tense.

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs ending in -yer
grammar_rules.summary: The 'y' changes to 'i' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (j'envoie, nous envoyons).
grammar_rules.explanation: In verbs ending in -oyer and -uyer (envoyer, nettoyer, essuyer), 'y' changes to 'i' before a silent 'e' (boot pattern: je, tu, il, ils). For -ayer verbs (payer), both 'i' and 'y' forms are accepted (je paie / je paye).

steps: Change 'y' to 'i' in singular and 3rd person plural forms
Keep 'y' in nous and vous forms

exceptions: payer allows both je paie and je paye

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs with -e- + consonant + -er
grammar_rules.summary: The silent 'e' changes to 'è' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (j'achète, nous achetons).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like acheter, emmener, lever, peser add a grave accent (è) in the boot forms (je, tu, il, ils) where the ending is silent.

steps: Add accent grave 'è' to stem in je, tu, il, ils
Keep unaccented 'e' in nous and vous

common_mistakes.explanation: Nous and vous keep the unaccented stem.

grammar_rules.title: Stem change in verbs with -é- + consonant + -er
grammar_rules.summary: The 'é' changes to 'è' in all forms except 'nous' and 'vous' (je répète, nous répétons).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like répéter, célébrer, espérer, préférer change the acute accent (é) to a grave accent (è) in the boot forms.

steps: Change 'é' to 'è' in je, tu, il, ils

grammar_rules.title: Verbs ending in -eler and -eter doubling consonant
grammar_rules.summary: Verbs like appeler and jeter double the 'l' or 't' before silent endings (j'appelle, je jette).
grammar_rules.explanation: Verbs like appeler, rappeler, renouveler, épeler double the 'l' (ll) in boot forms. Verbs like jeter double the 't' (tt). Nous and vous keep a single consonant.

steps: Double 'l' or 't' in je, tu, il, ils
Single 'l' or 't' in nous and vous

exceptions: geler and acheter take accent grave instead of doubling consonant

grammar_rules.title: Present tense for general statements and ongoing actions
grammar_rules.summary: French present translates simple present, present continuous, and emphatic present in English.
grammar_rules.explanation: In French, 'Valérie parle' translates to 'Valérie speaks', 'Valérie is speaking', and 'Valérie does speak'. There is no separate progressive form with 'être' unless using the construction 'être en train de'.
notes: Do not say 'elle est parlant' for 'she is speaking'.

common_mistakes.explanation: French does not use être + present participle for ongoing actions.

grammar_rules.title: Present tense expressing near future
grammar_rules.summary: The present tense can express an action planned or happening in the near future.
grammar_rules.explanation: Just as in English, a present tense verb combined with a future time marker indicates planned future action: 'Il part demain soir' (He is leaving tomorrow evening).
usage_conditions: Planned upcoming events with time adverbs

grammar_rules.title: Present tense for habitual actions
grammar_rules.summary: Describes habits, routines, and repeated actions in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Use the present tense with frequency markers like 'tous les jours', 'd'habitude', 'toujours' to describe habitual events.

grammar_rules.title: Historical and dramatic present
grammar_rules.summary: Used to recount historical facts or past events with dramatic immediacy.
grammar_rules.explanation: In narratives and history, the present tense makes past events feel vivid and immediate: 'Flaubert publie Madame Bovary et c'est le scandale!'.

grammar_rules.title: Continuous action with être en train de + infinitive
grammar_rules.summary: Expresses that an action is currently in progress ('in the middle of doing something').
grammar_rules.explanation: To explicitly emphasize that an action is in progress at this exact moment, use conjugated être + en train de + infinitive: 'Je suis en train de parler' (I am in the middle of talking).

steps: Add 'en train de' (or 'en train d'' before vowel)

notes: Use 'd'' before vowel or silent h (en train d'étudier).

common_mistakes.correct: Je suis en train de parler
common_mistakes.explanation: Use être en train de + infinitive, not present participle.

grammar_rules.title: Action continuing into the present with depuis, il y a... que, ça fait... que
grammar_rules.summary: Use the French present tense with 'depuis' for actions that began in the past and continue in the present.
grammar_rules.explanation: Unlike English which uses the present perfect ('I have been living here for three years'), French uses the PRESENT tense with 'depuis': 'J'habite à Nice depuis trois ans'. Questions use 'depuis quand' (since when) or 'depuis combien de temps' (for how long).

patterns: [VERBE AU PRÉSENT] + depuis + [DURÉE / POINT DE DÉPART]

usage_conditions: Ongoing action initiated in the past
notes: If the action is completed and no longer continues, use passé composé + pendant/il y a, not depuis.

common_mistakes.wrong: J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans (when still living there)
common_mistakes.explanation: In French, use the present tense if the action is still ongoing.

spelling_change_notes: accent grave è in boot forms

english: to be in the middle of doing something
to be doing something right now
usage_notes: Used to emphasize ongoing actions in the present or past
Asks for duration of an action still in progress
Asks for the starting date/moment of an action still in progress
Synonym for depuis when stating ongoing duration at sentence start
Very common spoken alternative to depuis

The present indicative is used in a number of ways: ◆ To make a general statement and to describe ongoing actions in the present. It can be translated in three different ways. Valérie parle à son ami Ludovic. Valérie is talking (talks, does talk) to her friend Ludovic. Il regarde les étoiles dans le ciel. He is looking (looks, does look) at the stars in the sky. ◆ To express a close future Il part demain soir. He’ll leave tomorrow night. On parle de cela en fin de semaine. We’ll discuss this at the end of the week. ◆ To express a habitual action Tous les jours, le soleil se lève. The sun rises every day. D’habitude, j’achète la viande dans Usually I buy meat in this butcher shop. cette boucherie. ◆ To describe a past action closely connected to the present Claude revient d’Asie et c’est la Claude just returned from Asia and pagaille au bureau! chaos started in the office! À peine rentrés et les problèmes They have just come back and the problems commencent déjà. have already started. ◆ To express a historical fact Flaubert publie Madame Bovary et Flaubert published Madame Bovary and c’est le scandale! the scandal broke out! Le président arrive en Chine et c’est The president arrived in China and it la débâcle! was a complete disaster! ◆ To describe past events more dramatically La reine avance vers le trône. The queen moved toward the throne. Et son pire ennemi entre dans la salle. And his worst enemy walked into the room. ◆ To express an action in the process, être en train de  the infi nitive form of the verb is used. questions.prompt: Elle mange une omelette aux champignons. One more use of the present tense: depuis The present tense is used to express an action that began in the past and continues in the present. Note that in English, the past tense is used. There are different ways to formulate the questions, using either depuis, il y a... que, cela (ça) fait... que. Let’s start with depuis. To ask a question about the duration of an action, use depuis quand (since when) or depuis combien de temps (how long). Depuis combien de temps habites-tu How long have you been living in Nice? à Nice? —J’habite à Nice depuis trois ans. —I have been living in Nice for three years. Depuis quand travaillez-vous chez How long have you been working at L’Oréal? L’Oréal? —Je travaille chez L’Oréal depuis —I have been working at L’Oréal for three trois mois. months. Il y a combien de temps que vous How long have you known Mr. Blier? connaissez M. Blier? —Il y a quelques années que je connais —I have known Mr. Blier for a few years. M. Blier. Ça fait combien de temps que vous How long have you had this dictionary? avez ce dictionnaire? —Ça fait cinq ans que j’ai ce —I have had this dictionary for five years. dictionnaire.
